title: Resistance, Compliance and Local Blood Flow

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Flow through any stretch of vessel equals the pressure drop across it divided by its {{c1::resistance}}: Q = ΔP / R.
cards.quote: the flow through any stretch of vessel equals the pressure drop across it divided by its resistance, Q = ΔP / R

cards.front: If the heart and the reflexes hold mean arterial pressure nearly steady, how does each tissue set its own blood flow?
cards.back: By setting the resistance of its own arterioles: flow to a tissue = (MAP − Pra) / that tissue's resistance, where Pra is right atrial pressure.
cards.quote: Each tissue then sets its own blood flow by setting the resistance of its own arterioles

cards.front: For vascular segments in series, why does each segment's share of the pressure drop equal its share of the resistance?
cards.back: The same flow passes every segment, and ΔP = Q × R for each one, so each segment's pressure drop is proportional to its resistance.
cards.quote: A segment's share of the pressure drop equals its share of the resistance.
cards.section: Where the pressure goes

cards.front: Glass micropipettes recorded pressure in single microvessels of cat tenuissimus muscle under anesthesia. Which vessels held most of the bed's resistance, and how much pressure did the capillary bed take?
cards.back: Arterioles 35 to 20 micrometres across were the principal source of resistance. The capillary bed proper took only about 15 percent of arterial pressure.
cards.quote: Arterioles 35 to 20 micrometres across were the principal source of resistance setting the pressure downstream.
cards.section: Where the pressure goes

cards.front: One capillary resists far more than one arteriole. Why does the capillary level of a skeletal-muscle bed still resist less than the arterioles?
cards.back: Each capillary is short and very many lie side by side, giving thousands of parallel paths, and parallel paths lower total resistance.
cards.why: This is a measured fact about muscle, not a law; the brain may differ.
cards.quote: so many lie side by side that the blood has thousands of narrow paths at once
cards.section: Where the pressure goes

cards.front: Why are arterioles the vessels where resistance can be adjusted?
cards.back: Their walls are rings of smooth muscle, and resistance goes as 1/r^4, so a small change in radius makes a large change in resistance. Capillaries have no smooth-muscle coat.
cards.quote: Their walls are rings of smooth muscle, and by Poiseuille's law resistance goes as 1/r^4, where r is the radius
cards.section: Where the pressure goes

cards.front: Illustrative values: mean arterial pressure 100 mmHg, right atrial pressure 4 mmHg, cardiac output 6 L per min. Find total peripheral resistance in mmHg min per L and in dyn s cm^-5.
cards.back: TPR = (100 − 4) / 6 = 96 / 6 = 16 mmHg min per L (Wood units). × 80 = 1,280 dyn s cm^-5.
cards.quote: TPR's unit, mmHg min per L, is the Wood unit; multiplying by 80 gives dyn s cm^-5
cards.section: Where the pressure goes

cards.front: Because small arteries and arterioles hold most of the resistance, total peripheral resistance rises and falls mainly with {{c1::arteriolar tone}}.
cards.quote: Because small arteries and arterioles hold most of the resistance, TPR rises and falls mainly with arteriolar tone.
cards.section: Where the pressure goes

cards.front: Resistances in parallel add as reciprocals, so n equal parallel paths {{c1::divide the resistance by n}}.
cards.back: Two equal paths halve it.
cards.quote: Two equal paths halve the resistance (n equal paths divide it by n).
cards.section: Beds in parallel share one pressure

cards.front: In a made-up model, three organ beds lie in parallel: 12, 12 and 6 mmHg min per L. What is their combined resistance?
cards.back: 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/12 + 1/12 + 2/12 = 4/12 = 1/3. Reciprocal: 3 mmHg min per L, lower than any single bed.
cards.quote: Step 2, take the reciprocal of the sum: R = 1 / 0.2 = 5 mmHg min per L.
cards.section: Beds in parallel share one pressure

cards.front: Under Poiseuille scaling, an arteriole's radius narrows by 20 percent with length unchanged. By what factor does its resistance change?
cards.back: R goes as 1/r^4. New R / old R = 1 / 0.8^4 = 1 / 0.41 ≈ 2.4, so resistance rises about 2.4-fold.
cards.quote: So a small change in radius makes a large change in resistance.
cards.section: Where the pressure goes

cards.front: Made-up resting values: heart rate 60 per min, stroke volume 70 mL, arterial pressure 110/70 mmHg, right atrial pressure 3 mmHg. Using the one-third rule, find cardiac output, MAP and TPR.
cards.back: CO = 60 × 0.070 = 4.2 L per min. PP = 40, so MAP = 70 + 40/3 = 83.3 mmHg. TPR = (83.3 − 3) / 4.2 ≈ 19.1 mmHg min per L.
cards.quote: CO = 75 per min x 0.080 L = 6.0 L per min.
cards.section: Worked problem: one muscle bed inside the whole circulation

cards.front: In a lumped model with no reflexes, one large vascular bed dilates while cardiac output stays fixed and no other bed constricts. What happens to MAP and to flow in the other beds, and why?
cards.back: MAP falls and the other beds lose flow. TPR falls, so at fixed output MAP = TPR × CO + Pra drops; the dilated bed takes a larger share and steals flow from the rest.
cards.quote: The dilating bed has stolen flow from the rest.
cards.section: Worked problem: one muscle bed inside the whole circulation

cards.front: Lumped model: muscle bed 30 and all other beds 30 mmHg min per L, in parallel, driving pressure (MAP − Pra) 90 mmHg. The muscle bed dilates to 6. What cardiac output holds the driving pressure at 90, and what flow do the other beds get?
cards.back: Before: TPR = 15, CO = 6 L per min, 3 to each bed. After: 1/6 + 1/30 = 6/30 = 0.2, TPR = 5. CO must be 90 / 5 = 18 L per min: muscle 15, others 90 / 30 = 3, unchanged.
cards.quote: To hold 93 mmHg at a TPR of 6.0, output must reach 90 / 6.0 = 15 L per min.
cards.section: Worked problem: one muscle bed inside the whole circulation

cards.front: A person with autonomic failure, who has lost sympathetic restraint, exercises large muscle groups. Predict arterial pressure and explain using the parallel-bed rule.
cards.back: Pressure falls. Muscle beds dilate and TPR drops; without a reflex rise in output and constriction of other beds, MAP = TPR × CO + Pra cannot be defended.
cards.why: Rests on the undefended case of the lumped model: a dilating bed lowers TPR and MAP unless output rises or other beds constrict.
cards.quote: when sympathetic restraint is lost, as in autonomic failure, pressure falls during large-muscle exercise
cards.section: Worked problem: one muscle bed inside the whole circulation

cards.front: Name the local signals that dilate arterioles when a tissue works harder.
cards.back: Adenosine, K+, CO2 and H+, and low O2 from the working tissue, and nitric oxide from the endothelium. No single signal does it.
cards.quote: adenosine, K+, CO2 and H+, and low O2 from the working tissue, and nitric oxide from the endothelium
cards.section: Tissues set their own flow

cards.front: How does hypoxia affect systemic arterioles compared with pulmonary arterioles?
cards.back: Hypoxia dilates systemic arterioles but constricts pulmonary arterioles.
cards.quote: One contrast to keep straight: hypoxia dilates systemic arterioles but constricts pulmonary arterioles
cards.section: Tissues set their own flow

cards.front: {{c1::Autoregulation}} holds a bed's flow relatively constant over a range of perfusion pressures while its metabolic demand is unchanged.
cards.quote: Autoregulation holds a bed's flow relatively constant over a range of perfusion pressures while its metabolic demand is unchanged.
cards.section: Autoregulation: the tap that holds flow steady

cards.front: Across the autoregulatory range, perfusion pressure rises. What must the arterioles do to keep flow steady, and why?
cards.back: Narrow. For Q = ΔP / R to stay put while ΔP rises, R must rise in proportion; as pressure falls they widen.
cards.quote: For Q = ΔP / R to stay put while ΔP rises, R must rise in proportion
cards.section: Autoregulation: the tap that holds flow steady

cards.front: The {{c1::myogenic response}} is the acute reaction of a small artery to a change in transmural pressure, the pressure across its wall.
cards.back: One mechanism of autoregulation; it answers pressure, not activity.
cards.quote: One mechanism is the myogenic response, the acute reaction of a small artery to a change in transmural pressure
cards.section: Autoregulation: the tap that holds flow steady

cards.front: Perfusion pressure to an autoregulating bed keeps falling, and its arterioles keep widening to hold flow. What happens once they are maximally dilated?
cards.back: Flow falls with pressure. This is the lower limit of autoregulation: R cannot fall further, and passive narrowing at low pressure makes flow fall even faster.
cards.quote: The pressure at which the resistance vessels are maximally dilated is the lower limit of autoregulation.
cards.section: Autoregulation: the tap that holds flow steady

cards.front: A fixed narrowing forms in the artery feeding an autoregulating bed. Predict flow at rest and at peak demand.
cards.back: Near normal at rest, low at peak demand. Downstream arterioles dilate to offset the narrowing, so they have spent part of their reserve and hit the lower limit sooner.
cards.quote: Those arterioles have already spent part of their dilation, so they reach the lower limit sooner
cards.section: A narrowing upstream: flow at rest, flow at full demand

cards.front: A patient with a fixed narrowing in a coronary artery develops a fast heart rate. Predict the effect on perfusion of the inner layers of the left ventricle, and give the rules it rests on.
cards.back: In the model, inner-layer perfusion worsens. Those layers are fed mainly in diastole, a fast rate shortens diastole more than systole, and arterioles beyond the narrowing have already spent part of their dilation.
cards.why: Combines the stenosis rule (reserve lost), systolic compression of inner vessels, and the shortening of diastole at fast rates.
cards.quote: In the heart, the inner layers of the left ventricle fare worst: systole squeezes their vessels, so they are fed mainly in diastole.
cards.section: A narrowing upstream: flow at rest, flow at full demand

cards.front: Robert Berne made isolated cat hearts and dogs hypoxic. Coronary resistance fell and the muscle released inosine and hypoxanthine. What did he propose?
cards.back: That adenosine, formed as ATP breaks down when oxygen supply falls short of use, diffuses to the arterioles and dilates them.
cards.quote: He proposed that adenosine, formed as ATP breaks down when oxygen supply falls short of use, diffuses to the arterioles and dilates them.
cards.section: Metabolic signals: Berne and adenosine

cards.front: What did later adenosine receptor blockade in dogs show about adenosine's role in coronary flow?
cards.back: Adenosine is a potent dilator, but its role is not evident unless oxygen delivery is compromised; other signals probably overlap.
cards.quote: found adenosine a potent dilator whose role is not evident unless oxygen delivery is compromised
cards.section: Metabolic signals: Berne and adenosine

cards.front: Design an experiment in an isolated perfused heart to test whether adenosine is needed to match coronary flow to oxygen demand.
cards.back: Raise demand (pacing or an inotrope) and separately lower supply; plot coronary flow against oxygen use. Repeat under adenosine receptor blockade, confirming the block abolishes the response to infused adenosine, and track coronary venous oxygen.
cards.why: If adenosine couples flow to demand, venous oxygen should fall with rising demand under blockade; release alone shows only sufficiency.
cards.quote: prove the block works by showing that the response to infused adenosine is lost
cards.section: Is adenosine necessary?

cards.front: A nitric oxide synthase inhibitor is infused into the brachial artery of healthy volunteers. Predict basal forearm flow and the dilations to acetylcholine and to glyceryl trinitrate, a nitric oxide donor.
cards.back: Basal flow halves; acetylcholine dilation is blunted; glyceryl trinitrate dilation is spared. In the forearm, continuous nitric oxide release holds resting arterioles partly dilated.
cards.quote: So in the forearm, resting arterioles are held partly dilated by continuous nitric oxide release.
cards.section: Nitric oxide sets resting tone

cards.front: Why is a rise in the heart's oxygen use met mainly by more coronary flow rather than more extraction?
cards.back: At rest the left ventricle already extracts 60 to 80 percent of delivered oxygen, so little extraction is left to call on.
cards.quote: At rest the left ventricle extracts 60 to 80 percent of delivered oxygen, so it has little extraction left to call on
cards.section: Who turns the tap: four circulations

cards.front: How do cerebral vessels respond to a rise and to a fall in arterial PCO2?
cards.back: A rise dilates them; a fall constricts them. They are very sensitive to arterial PCO2.
cards.quote: Cerebral vessels are very sensitive to arterial PCO2: a rise dilates them, a fall constricts them.
cards.section: Who turns the tap: four circulations

cards.front: What mainly controls skin blood flow, and through what?
cards.back: Body temperature, through nerves. In human whole-body heating, an estimated 80 to 90 percent of the dilation comes from a sympathetic active vasodilator system.
cards.quote: Skin flow follows body temperature more than skin metabolism.
cards.section: Who turns the tap: four circulations

cards.front: A person exercising a leg hard starts to hyperventilate, lowering arterial PCO2. Predict how cerebral arterioles respond.
cards.back: They constrict: cerebral vessels are very sensitive to arterial PCO2, and a fall constricts them.
cards.why: Brain flow follows arterial PCO2: a rise dilates, a fall constricts.
cards.quote: Cerebral vessels are very sensitive to arterial PCO2: a rise dilates them, a fall constricts them.
cards.section: Who turns the tap: four circulations

cards.front: {{c1::Compliance}} is how much a vessel stretches: how much volume it takes up for each step in pressure.
cards.quote: That is the job of compliance: how much a vessel stretches, how much volume it takes up for each step in pressure.
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: The heart ejects in spurts. How does arterial compliance keep capillary flow going between beats?
cards.back: During ejection the arteries fill faster than they drain, so their walls stretch; in diastole they recoil and keep capillary flow going.
cards.quote: During ejection the arteries fill faster than they drain, so their walls stretch; in diastole they recoil and keep capillary flow going.
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: At rest, stroke volume is 72 mL and aortic pulse pressure is 48 mmHg. Estimate total arterial compliance.
cards.back: 72 / 48 = 1.5 mL per mmHg. It is an estimate, not compliance itself, because some blood runs off during ejection.
cards.quote: At rest, stroke volume divided by aortic pulse pressure is a useful estimate of total arterial compliance.
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: Why is mean arterial pressure estimated as diastolic pressure plus one third of pulse pressure, not the average of systolic and diastolic?
cards.back: MAP is the time average of the pressure curve. At resting heart rates diastole fills roughly two thirds of the cycle, so pressure spends most of its time near diastolic.
cards.quote: At resting heart rates diastole fills roughly two thirds of the cycle, so the pressure spends most of its time near diastolic.
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: A resting aortic pressure reads 135/75 mmHg. Estimate mean arterial pressure with the one-third rule, and compare it with the simple average.
cards.back: PP = 60 mmHg. MAP ≈ 75 + 60/3 = 95 mmHg, below the simple average of 105.
cards.quote: That gives the standard estimate: start at diastolic pressure (DBP) and add one third of the pulse pressure (PP).
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: Where does the one-third rule for mean arterial pressure fail, and in which direction?
cards.back: At fast heart rates. Diastole shortens more than systole, so the true mean sits higher than the rule gives.
cards.quote: At fast heart rates diastole shortens more than systole, so the true mean sits higher than this rule gives
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: Arterial pressure is 110/70 mmHg. Arterial compliance halves while stroke volume and mean pressure stay the same. Predict the new systolic and diastolic pressures.
cards.back: About 137/57. Pulse pressure doubles to 80; MAP stays 83.3, so DBP = 83.3 − 80/3 = 56.7 and SBP = 56.7 + 80 = 136.7 mmHg.
cards.why: Mean pressure depends on cardiac output and resistance, not compliance; figures are approximate because the one-third rule shifts with waveform.
cards.quote: Mean pressure depends on cardiac output and resistance, not on compliance.
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: In longitudinal data on untreated adults, after age 50 to 60 diastolic pressure declined, pulse pressure rose steeply and mean pressure levelled off. What does this pattern suggest?
cards.back: Large-artery stiffening. Lower compliance widens the pulse, raising systolic and lowering diastolic pressure while the mean, set by output and resistance, holds.
cards.quote: after age 50 to 60 diastolic pressure declined, pulse pressure rose steeply and mean pressure levelled off
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: In a lumped model, arterial compliance falls while mean pressure and stroke volume are unchanged. Predict the effect on the pressure that feeds the inner layers of the left ventricle.
cards.back: In the model, diastolic pressure falls, so the driving pressure for diastolic feeding falls. The inner layers are fed mainly in diastole, because systole squeezes their vessels.
cards.why: Combines the compliance prediction (diastolic down, mean unchanged) with diastolic feeding of the inner left ventricle.
cards.quote: So 120/80 becomes about 147/67: systolic and pulse pressure up, diastolic down, mean unchanged.
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: In humans, about what share of the blood do veins hold, and how compliant are they compared with arteries?
cards.back: About 70 percent of the blood; roughly 24 times more compliant than arteries in the standard textbook estimate.
cards.quote: In humans they hold about 70 percent of the blood and are roughly 24 times more compliant than arteries
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: Distinguish stressed from unstressed venous volume, and say what venoconstriction does to them.
cards.back: Unstressed volume fills a vessel without stretching its wall; stressed volume stretches it and makes pressure. Venoconstriction shifts unstressed into stressed volume without adding blood.
cards.quote: Unstressed volume fills a vessel without stretching its wall; stressed volume stretches it and makes pressure.
cards.section: Compliance: the pulse the rule leaves out

cards.front: Under Poiseuille's law, compare one 5-micrometre capillary with one 20-micrometre arteriole that is twice as long. How many times more does the capillary resist?
cards.back: R goes as length / r^4. Radius ratio 4, so 4^4 = 256; half the length gives 256 × 0.5 = 128 times.
cards.quote: one capillary resists about 128 times more than one arteriole
cards.section: Why capillaries lose in muscle
